source_metadata.title: Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry

extraction_limitations: Atoms represent independently reviewable claims selected from the preprint; the bibliography itself was not atomized.
Figure 12 is represented as a qualitative result because the plotted per-task point values are not tabulated in the source text.
No funding, conflict-of-interest, or formal data-availability statement was located in the paper text, so no atoms of those kinds were created.
Efficiency measurements are preserved as reported; the paper notes an eager-attention, bf16, batch-size-1 decode measurement protocol in Appendix H.
The H2Share appendix extension is included selectively for its distinct method and ablation claims rather than exhaustively atomizing every equation/proof step.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study asks whether frozen query-key weights alone can provide a useful prior for attention-head function without runtime attention scores, calibration prompts, or additional training.
AoH defines a head-specific kernel attention matrix M_h = W_K^T W_Q as the frozen query-key matching operator for an attention head.
AoH measures each head by the effective rank of the singular-value distribution of M_h, computed as the exponential of the Shannon entropy of normalized nonzero singular values.
Heads with concentrated low-effective-rank spectra are associated with retrieval-style attention, whereas heads with diffuse high-effective-rank spectra are associated with streaming-style attention.
AoH assigns low-effective-rank heads to global full attention and high-effective-rank heads to sink-and-recent streaming attention.
The nonzero singular spectrum of M_h is obtained from the d_head-dimensional proxy C_h=(W_QW_Q^T)(W_KW_K^T), whose eigenvalues equal the squared nonzero singular values of M_h.
For Qwen2.5-7B, the optimized d_head-space computation is estimated at approximately 4.6×10^7 operations versus 5.9×10^10 operations for constructing the full matrix.
For grouped-query attention, AoH averages per-query-head effective ranks within each KV group and ranks KV groups by the resulting mean score.
Within each layer, the lowest-effective-rank KV groups are labeled retrieval groups and the remaining groups are labeled streaming groups, with all query heads in a group inheriting the group label.
Before deployment, query, key, and value projection channels are reordered so retrieval and streaming heads or groups are contiguous, avoiding scatter/gather cache management.

During decoding, retrieval heads attend to layer-specific full K/V states while streaming heads attend only to fixed sink and recent-window K/V caches; outputs are concatenated before the shared output projection.
During chunked prefill, retrieval heads retain full prefix K/V states while streaming heads evict all but sink and recent tokens after each chunk.

With fixed streaming-cache sizes and chunk size K, AoH reduces streaming-head prefill complexity from O(T^2) to O(TK), bounds persistent streaming K/V storage by O(s_sink+s_recent), and peak working memory by O(K).
The primary evaluation uses LongBench, comprising 21 long-context tasks across six categories, with the arithmetic mean over all 21 tasks as the primary aggregate score.

population.label: LongBench: 21 tasks across single-document QA, multi-document QA, summarization, few-shot learning, synthetic retrieval, and code completion

atoms.canonical_statement: Qwen2.5-7B is evaluated as a 28-layer model with 28 query heads and 4 KV heads, corresponding to GQA group size 7.

population.label: Qwen2.5-7B: 28 layers, 28 Q-heads, 4 KV-heads, GQA group size 7

atoms.canonical_statement: Qwen3-8B is evaluated as a 36-layer model with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads.
Unless otherwise stated, streaming heads use 128 sink tokens and a 256-token recent window.
LongBench evaluations use a maximum sequence length of 32,768 tokens and greedy decoding.
The comparison set includes Full Attention, H2O, SnapKV, Quest, DuoAttention, random head selection, and reversed effective-rank selection.
For LongBench budget matching, AoH and DuoAttention keep full 32K cache for 50% retrieval heads and a 384-token cache for 50% streaming heads, yielding about 50.6% storage and attended-KV budgets.

The passkey study on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct uses 32K contexts, 100 samples, passkeys inserted at 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% depth, and compares Low-ER-first, High-ER-first, and random conversion to streaming attention.
Per-head average attention-distance patterns on Qwen2.5-7B remain structurally stable across context lengths from 4K to 100K.
Lower-effective-rank heads tend to attend farther into context, whereas higher-effective-rank heads are more local.
Converting high-effective-rank heads to sink-and-recent attention has little effect on passkey retrieval, whereas converting low-effective-rank heads causes retrieval accuracy to collapse rapidly.
On Qwen3-8B at 32K context, effective rank has a Spearman correlation of -0.32 with average attended distance across heads.
On Qwen3-8B at 32K context, effective rank has a Spearman correlation of -0.23 with attention entropy across heads.

atoms.canonical_statement: On Qwen3-8B at 32K context, effective rank has a Spearman correlation of -0.31 with attention mass assigned to tokens more than 8K positions away.
At 50% sparsity on Qwen3-8B, AoH scores 38.78 on LongBench versus 39.10 for Full Attention.
At 50% sparsity on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, AoH scores 47.55 on LongBench versus 48.65 for Full Attention.
At 50% sparsity on Qwen2.5-7B, AoH scores 34.95 on LongBench versus 37.94 for Full Attention.
At 50% sparsity on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, AoH scores 48.79 on LongBench versus 50.95 for Full Attention.
On Qwen3-8B, AoH exceeds the best reported sparse baseline average (Quest, 36.76) by 2.02 LongBench points at the matched evaluation setting.

atoms.canonical_statement: The abstract reports up to a 41.4% reduction in prefill latency with AoH.
The abstract reports up to a 66.0% reduction in decode latency with AoH.
The abstract reports a 50.0% KV-cache memory reduction at 256K tokens with AoH.
H2Share extends AoH with three offline steps: head or KV-group classification, anchor–reuse block assignment, and cross-layer head/group mapping.
H2Share transfers only selected token indices across layers; each reuse layer computes its own key and value vectors at the borrowed positions.
H2Share maps each reuse retrieval head to the functionally closest anchor retrieval head using the normalized Frobenius inner product between kernel attention matrices, computed in d_head space.
The shared-KV H2Share ablation is reported to collapse because of cross-layer projection-space mismatch, motivating index-only sharing.
Figure 12 reports that H2Share provides a better KV-budget–accuracy trade-off than the compared configurations on the shown LongBench tasks.
For GQA, retention decisions are made at KV-group level so sparse cache partitioning does not destroy grouped-query storage efficiency.
The evaluation is focused on decoder-only LLMs with standard attention variants, and does not exhaustively test encoder-decoder models, multimodal LLMs, or heavily modified attention mechanisms.
AoH uses a manually selected fixed sparsity budget that is held constant across layers; adaptive layer-, model-, or deployment-specific budgets are not evaluated.

The authors conclude that frozen query-key spectral geometry provides a simple data-free prior for retrieval versus streaming head roles and can support sparse long-context inference without additional training.
The authors propose AoH as an extensible head prior that can be combined with existing KV-cache compression or token-selection methods.
